problem: End-to-end learned exploration policies such as Chen et al. 2019 need imitation learning and many millions of frames. They still underperform classical geometry-based exploration, forget explored areas over long horizons, and get stuck locally. Prior simulation setups also assume noise-free motion or known pose, which makes pose estimation trivial and unrealistic.
motivation: Exploration (maximizing coverage in a fixed time budget) is a core subproblem of navigation in unknown environments. Learning offers three benefits: flexible input modality (map from RGB alone), robustness to state-estimation error, and exploiting structural regularities of layouts. The key observation is that these benefits operate at different time scales, so learning can be factored into a classical, hierarchical navigation pipeline instead of one monolithic policy, which sidesteps the sample complexity of end-to-end RL.
key_idea: Put learned modules inside a classical navigation pipeline, interfaced through an explicit 2D map and an analytic Fast Marching planner: a Neural SLAM module (RGB + noisy odometry → obstacle/explored map + corrected pose), an RL global policy that picks long-term goals on the map, and an IL local policy that reaches planner-generated short-term goals from RGB.
insight:
Hierarchy shortens the effective RL horizon: the global policy acts only every 25 steps, and memory lives in an explicit map. This is why ANS keeps improving over long episodes while end-to-end RL baselines get stuck in local areas. Ablations (Table 2, Gibson val):
- Global policy vs. classical frontier exploration (FBE, closest-frontier): the learned global policy matters in large scenes (%Cov 0.862 vs 0.782) but not in small ones (0.983 vs 0.982). FBE wastes time on corners and small areas behind furniture.
- Pose estimator: removing it drops large-scene coverage to 0.771 because odometry drift accumulates. Yet overall coverage (0.916) still beats the best baseline (0.789), so the gain is not mainly from the extra pose supervision.
- Local policy: gives a small gain over a deterministic plan follower (0.948 vs 0.941) by correcting mapping false positives, e.g. walking over a carpet mapped as an obstacle.
Because the SLAM module and local policy are task-invariant, swapping the global policy for the given goal transfers ANS to PointGoal with essentially no loss (0.950/0.846 vs 0.951/0.848 when trained on PointGoal).
method: Realistic noise models: a LoCoBot with a Hokuyo LiDAR as ground truth yields 600 datapoints per action. From these, 6 Gaussian mixture models (actuation and sensor noise for Forward 25 cm, Turn L/R 10°) are fit over (x, y, o) with components chosen on validation, then inserted into Habitat.

Map representation: a 2×M×M geocentric map (obstacle probability, explored probability) at 5 cm cells; the agent starts at the map center facing east. M=480 (24 m) in training, 960 (48 m) at evaluation.

Neural SLAM module: the Mapper (ResNet18 conv → 2 FC → 3 deconv) predicts a 2×64×64 egocentric top-down obstacle/explored map (3.2 m range) from 128×128 RGB. The Pose Estimator (3 conv + 3 FC) compares the previous egocentric map, spatially transformed by the odometry pose change, with the current one to predict a corrected relative pose. The egocentric map is transformed by the estimated pose and aggregated into the global map by channel-wise pooling. Supervised with BCE on GT projections from GT depth and MSE on GT pose.

Global policy: input is a 4-channel map tensor (obstacles, explored, current position, visited locations), given as a local G×G crop stacked with a max-pooled full map (8×240×240), plus an orientation embedding. A 5-layer CNN + 3 FC outputs a long-term goal every 25 steps. Trained with PPO; reward = 0.02 × increase in coverage (m²).

Planner: the Fast Marching Method on the predicted obstacle map, with unexplored cells treated as free. It computes a path to the long-term goal and emits as short-term goal the farthest point within 0.25 m on the path.

Local policy: pretrained ResNet18 + FC + GRU on RGB, with binned relative distance/angle to the short-term goal and binned timestep as embeddings. Outputs forward/turn-left/turn-right and is trained by behavioral cloning. All modules are trained simultaneously with separate parameters, for 10M frames on 72 Gibson scenes.
PointGoal transfer: the global policy is fixed to output the PointGoal coordinates as the long-term goal, reusing the exploration-trained SLAM module and local policy with no further training.

setting.backbone: Modular ANS: ImageNet-pretrained ResNet18 Mapper + CNN Pose Estimator (supervised), 5-layer CNN Global Policy (PPO), ResNet18+GRU Local Policy (behavioral cloning), with an analytic FMM planner; all trained by the authors
setting.training_data: Habitat Gibson train split (72 scenes, one per parallel thread), 10M frames, with LoCoBot-derived actuation/sensor noise models. Supervision comes from GT depth-projected egocentric maps, GT pose (Pose Estimator), a GT-map coverage reward (Global Policy) and planner-derived actions (Local Policy). No extra web or synthetic data.
setting.observation: monocular RGB 128×128 + noisy base odometry (3-DoF pose change); depth only as training supervision (the RGB-D Habitat Challenge track uses depth input)
setting.action_space: low-level MOVE_FORWARD 0.25 m / TURN_LEFT / TURN_RIGHT 10° with noisy actuation (PointGoal adds STOP); internally the global policy predicts long-term goals and the FMM planner produces short-term goals
setting.privileged: none at test time (noisy odometry only; GT map/pose used only for training supervision)

numbers_note: All metrics are printed as fractions (e.g. 0.948) and converted here to 0-100 (94.8); Cov in m² is kept as printed. Table 3's caption mistakenly says 'Exploration task' but reports PointGoal Succ/SPL. Coverage-vs-steps curves (Fig. 3, Fig. 10) and PointGoal performance vs. geodesic distance / GED ratio (Fig. 7) are given only as figures. A sample-efficiency number ('0.789/0.703 SPL/Succ at only 1 million frames') is omitted because its metric order is ambiguous. The exploration benchmark is the Chen et al. 2019 coverage task on Habitat Gibson/MP3D, not a canonical named benchmark. Real-world LoCoBot transfer is qualitative only.
results:
Exploration, Gibson val (after 10M training frames): ANS reaches 32.701 m² / 0.948 coverage vs 24.863 m² / 0.789 for the strongest end-to-end baseline (RL+Res18+ProjDepth, after Chen et al. 2019). On MP3D test it reaches 73.281 m² / 0.521 vs 54.775 m² / 0.378.

PointGoal: transferred to PointGoal with no extra training, ANS gets Succ/SPL 0.950/0.846 on Gibson val vs 0.827/0.730 for CMP, with larger margins on MP3D and on the Hard-Dist/Hard-GEDR sets. It is reported as >75× more sample-efficient than the best RL baseline.

Habitat Challenge: ANS won the CVPR 2019 Habitat PointGoal Challenge in both tracks, with SPL 0.805 (RGB) and 0.948 (RGB-D).
limitations: Mapping errors (e.g. false-positive obstacles such as carpets) propagate to the planner and cause failures; a PointGoal failure case is attributed to mapping error.

Training needs privileged supervision from GT depth projections, GT maps (coverage reward) and GT pose (Pose Estimator). The map is purely geometric 2D occupancy, with no semantics (left to future work).
Real-world transfer is shown only qualitatively on one apartment with a LoCoBot; evaluation is otherwise in simulation.
